title: The seven beggars
hookLine: Rebbe Nachman's tale: beggars with apparent defects each reveal a hidden gift
tomorrow: why did the rabbi's son never reach his teacher?

lines: A CHIPPED MUG EVERYONE REACHES FOR.
cards: A thrift-store mug with a chip in the rim, and somehow it's the one everybody reaches for. Rebbe Nachman told a long tale built on that kind of surprise.

Two children, lost in a forest, are fed by beggars passing through: one blind, one deaf, one who stammers, one with a crooked neck, a hunchback, one with no hands, one with no feet. Years later the children marry.
And at the wedding feast the beggars come back, one each day, as the wedding gift. The gift turns out to be what each one has been hiding.

teach.b: Each beggar opens his flaw like a box. The blind one says: I'm not blind at all. It's that the whole time of this world isn't worth a glance to me.
He's so old he remembers further back than every elder at the feast. The deaf one isn't deaf either.
The world's noise is all about what's missing, and he just doesn't hear lack; to him, life is good. The one who stammers is a master of speech, so eloquent that the world's talk can't hold his words.
The one with the crooked neck has a perfect voice. The flaw is where the gift lives.
And each beggar blesses the young couple to be like him. Wishing a bride and groom blindness sounds like a curse, until you've heard what the blindness really was.
Here's the detail to tell a friend tonight: the tale breaks off.
The seventh beggar, the one with no feet, never gets his day. Tradition says Rebbe Nachman left it untold, and Breslov Hasidim say it waits for the days of the Messiah.
Once you've heard the tale, the beggars start turning up.
The kid who barely talks may be the one who listens hardest. The friend who never hears the gossip isn't missing anything. The tale doesn't pretend that real suffering is secretly fine.
It asks you to look twice before you decide what someone lacks.

how: Rebbe Nachman's tales are studied in Breslov communities and beyond, read aloud and discussed for their hidden meanings; 'The Seven Beggars' is often read slowly, one beggar's day at a time.

o: a tale of beggars whose flaws each hide a gift
a teaching on seven kinds of charity to give
a list of guests a wedding host must feed first

games.q: who's hiding what — tap the pairs.
p: remembers further back than any elder

s: the tale ends with all seven beggars telling their stories
it breaks off: the beggar with no feet never gets his day.
the blind beggar says he isn't blind at all
the whole time of this world isn't worth a glance to him.
the tale teaches that every hardship is secretly a blessing
it asks you to look twice at what someone seems to lack; it doesn't pretend suffering away.

games.q: a new kid on your team never jokes around, and people call him boring. you're picking a partner for a big project. what would the seven beggars suggest?
o: pick him, and find out what the quiet might be hiding.
pick him out of kindness, so he isn't the one left over.
skip him; a quiet partner will slow the whole thing down.
games.why: in the tale, each beggar's flaw is where his gift lives. not pity, not dismissal: look twice.

practice: Pick up one object near you with a flaw: a chipped mug, a scuffed shoe, a phone with a cracked corner. Hold it for the sit and turn it slowly, letting your fingers find the flaw and stay there.
Ask what the flaw shows that a perfect one couldn't: years of use, a fall survived, a story no other one has.

wordCard.voice: The seven beggars: Rebbe Nachman's tale of beggars whose flaws each hide a gift, told one a day at a wedding, the seventh still untold.

orig.note: Hebrew: seven beggars, from the tale's Hebrew title; the tales were told in Yiddish and printed with Hebrew.

carryVoice: Keep this one: the hidden gift, sitting right where you'd only see the flaw. See you soon.
